example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、日[ひ]が出[で]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 窓から日が入る。
example_sentences.english: The sun comes in through the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から日[ひ]が入[はい]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はいい日です。
example_sentences.english: Today is a nice day.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はいい日[ひ]です。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 月（つき）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already carry this character as the <kanji>moon</kanji> kanji, and the <vocabulary>moon</vocabulary> word asks nothing more of it: same shape, same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: At night Suki the skier presses her goggles to the tall window with two bars and sighs <reading>ski</reading>, <reading>つき</reading>, because the pale <vocabulary form="月">moon</vocabulary> behind the glass has lit up the slope.

example_sentences.japanese: 夜、月を見ます。
example_sentences.english: At night, I look at the moon.
example_sentences.furigana: 夜[よる]、月[つき]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 空に月があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a moon in the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[そら]に月[つき]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で月を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the moon in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で月[つき]を見[み]ます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 動（どう）＋物（ぶつ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the farm the nameless <kanji>thing</kanji> in the yard gets written off as junk. The one that <kanji>moves</kanji> itself to a warm corner with nobody pushing it is an <vocabulary>animal</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で動物を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the animals in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で動[どう]物[ぶつ]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: この動物は猫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is this animal a cat?
example_sentences.furigana: この動[どう]物[ぶつ]は猫[ねこ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は動物の本を買います。
example_sentences.english: My little sister buys a book about animals.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は動[どう]物[ぶつ]の本[ほん]を買[か]います。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 色（いろ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take it all out and the world is a grey photocopy. The red of a stop sign or the green of a leaf, dropped back in, is <vocabulary>color</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tourist fans out a stack of <reading>Euro</reading> notes, one orange, one purple, one blue, far louder than the grey money back home, and laughs 「<reading>いろ</reading>」. Whatever makes one note orange and the next blue is <vocabulary>color</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この服の色はいいです。
example_sentences.english: This color of clothes is nice.
example_sentences.furigana: この服[ふく]の色[いろ]はいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: どの色を買いますか。
example_sentences.english: Which color will you buy?
example_sentences.furigana: どの色[いろ]を買[か]いますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 空の色を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I'm looking at the color of the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[そら]の色[いろ]を見[み]ます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 赤（あか）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>red</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> word are one and the same character, so the meaning simply carries over.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this reading in 赤ちゃん, so the word for <vocabulary>red</vocabulary> is just <reading>あか</reading> again.

example_sentences.japanese: この花は赤いです。
example_sentences.english: This flower is red.
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は赤[あか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤いシャツを買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a red shirt.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]いシャツを買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あれは赤い帽子です。
example_sentences.english: That one over there is a red hat.
example_sentences.furigana: あれは赤[あか]い帽[ぼう]子[し]です。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 青（あお）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Standing on its own, the <kanji>blue</kanji> kanji is the whole <vocabulary>blue</vocabulary> word, and the sense does not shift.
items.reading_mnemonic: Holding a fresh sprout up against the moon, a gardener pricks his thumb and yelps <reading>ow</reading>, <reading>あお</reading>, as the leaves turn the eerie shade of the moonlit sky: <vocabulary form="青">blue</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の空は青いです。
example_sentences.english: Today's sky is blue.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の空[そら]は青[あお]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 青い帽子を買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll buy a blue hat.
example_sentences.furigana: 青[あお]い帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: このペンは青いです。
example_sentences.english: This pen is blue.
example_sentences.furigana: このペンは青[あお]いです。

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 茶（ちゃ）on'yomi ＋ 色（いろ）kun'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a cup of <kanji>tea</kanji> to stew until it is almost black, and the <kanji>color</kanji> it stains the rim, the tablecloth, and your fingers is <vocabulary>brown</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: このコートは茶色です。
example_sentences.english: This coat is brown.
example_sentences.furigana: このコートは茶[ちゃ]色[いろ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の髪は茶色です。
example_sentences.english: My hair is brown.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたくし]の髪[かみ]は茶[ちゃ]色[いろ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 茶色のシャツを買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a brown shirt.
example_sentences.furigana: 茶[ちゃ]色[いろ]のシャツを買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 大（おお）＋きい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>big</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> word are the same character. The kana tail ending in い is the part that makes it an adjective, and every い adjective after this works the same way.
items.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman flings his arms out wide and plants his legs far apart to show how <vocabulary form="大きい">big</vocabulary> the fish was that swallowed his boat key, wailing <reading>oh, oh, key</reading>, <reading>おおきい</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: This room is big.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 大きい箱を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a big box.
example_sentences.furigana: 大[おお]きい箱[ばこ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain over there is big.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は大[おお]きいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 新（あたら）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>new</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>new</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character with the same meaning. The kana on the end finish in い, and that い is what marks it an adjective, as every い adjective does.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcutter swings his axe into the standing tree and gasps at the pale wood laid bare, so <reading>utterly shiny</reading>, <reading>あたらしい</reading>, that it looks brand <vocabulary form="新しい">new</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new book.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: この家は新しいです。
example_sentences.english: This house is new.
example_sentences.furigana: この家[いえ]は新[あたら]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a new movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sink your teeth into a perfectly ripe peach and the only sound you can make is a long, helpless <reading>eee</reading>. That squeal is 「<reading>いい</reading>」, and it means the peach is <vocabulary>good</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この料理はいいです。
example_sentences.english: This dish is good.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]はいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は来なくていいよ。
example_sentences.english: You don't have to come tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は来[こ]なくていいよ。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はいい天気です。
example_sentences.english: The weather is nice today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はいい天[てん]気[き]です。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 女（おんな）＋の＋人（ひと）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The door meant for any <kanji>person</kanji> gets repainted with a <kanji>woman</kanji> stick figure, so now it specifies exactly which <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary> may enter.
items.description: 女 alone can sound blunt when pointing at a specific woman; 女の人 is the everyday, polite way to say it in conversation.

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は医者です。
example_sentences.english: That woman is a doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は女の人と話します。
example_sentences.english: I talk with a woman.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたくし]は女[おんな]の人[ひと]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の人が公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: A woman is going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の人[ひと]が公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 白（しろ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>white</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>white</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning carries straight across with nothing added.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny rower paddles across the drop of milk under its spark of light, and as <reading>she rows</reading>, grunting <reading>しろ</reading>, her oars come up dripping bright <vocabulary form="白">white</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この紙は白いです。
example_sentences.english: This paper is white.
example_sentences.furigana: この紙[かみ]は白[しろ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 白い花を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought white flowers.
example_sentences.furigana: 白[しろ]い花[はな]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: どれが白いですか。
example_sentences.english: Which one is white?
example_sentences.furigana: どれが白[しろ]いですか。

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 市（し）.
items.mnemonic_text: The settlement grown past a town: shi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>city</kanji> kanji standing on its own is the whole word, so this <vocabulary>city</vocabulary> means exactly what the kanji does.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこの市の図書館で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read books at this city's library.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたくし]はこの市[し]の図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に友達と市の公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: On the weekend I hang out with a friend at the city park.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に友[とも]達[だち]と市[し]の公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 先月、家族とあの市へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: Last month I went to that city with my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]、家[か]族[ぞく]とあの市[し]へ行[い]きました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 店（みせ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single narrow room: a counter worn smooth by elbows, a bell that jingles when the door swings, shelves of goods each wearing a price tag. That is a <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every shelf in the place is a <reading>messy</reading> landslide of jars and tins, and prising one purchase out of that heap is what buying from a <vocabulary>shop</vocabulary>, a <reading>みせ</reading>, feels like.

example_sentences.japanese: この店は安いです。
example_sentences.english: This shop is cheap.
example_sentences.furigana: この店[みせ]は安[やす]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は店で本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a book at the shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたくし]は店[みせ]で本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達とあの店に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm going to that shop with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]とあの店[みせ]に行[い]きます。

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 台（だい）on'yomi ＋ 所（どころ）kun'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A squat stone <kanji>stand</kanji>, the kind built to hold up a bronze statue, gets shoved into the one <kanji>place</kanji> you cook. That corner is now the <vocabulary>kitchen</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は台所に入ります。
example_sentences.english: I go into the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたくし]は台[だい]所[どころ]に入[はい]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 台所でお茶を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink tea in the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 台[だい]所[どころ]でお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 台所の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the kitchen window.
example_sentences.furigana: 台[だい]所[どころ]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — お＋手（て）＋洗（あら）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The room set aside for you to <kanji>wash</kanji> your <kanji>hand</kanji> in is the one polite people call the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: お手洗いはあそこです。
example_sentences.english: The restroom is over there.
example_sentences.furigana: お手[て]洗[あら]いはあそこです。

example_sentences.japanese: お手洗いに行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the restroom.
example_sentences.furigana: お手[て]洗[あら]いに行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: コンビニのお手洗いに入ります。
example_sentences.english: I'm going into the convenience store restroom.
example_sentences.furigana: コンビニのお手[て]洗[あら]いに入[はい]ります。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 風（かぜ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This character is an old friend by now: the <kanji>wind</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>wind</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so nothing about the meaning changes.
items.reading_mnemonic: One slash of air lifts a beetle off the picnic table along with the strip of <reading>gauze</reading> it sat on, and the gauze snaps out flat: 「<reading>かぜ</reading>」, real <vocabulary form="風">wind</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は風が寒いです。
example_sentences.english: Today the wind is cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は風[かぜ]が寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 窓から風が入る。
example_sentences.english: Wind comes in through the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から風[かぜ]が入[はい]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 海の風がいいです。
example_sentences.english: The ocean breeze feels nice.
example_sentences.furigana: 海[うみ]の風[かぜ]がいいです。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 料（りょう）＋理（り）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Raw <kanji>materials</kanji> on the counter mean nothing until you add <kanji>logic</kanji> about heat, water and timing. That worked-out plan for the ingredients is <vocabulary>cooking</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この料理はおいしいです。
example_sentences.english: This dish is delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]はおいしいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎日料理をします。
example_sentences.english: My mom cooks every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]日[にち]料[りょう]理[り]をします。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達の料理を食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate my friend's cooking.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]の料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 黒（くろ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This <vocabulary>black</vocabulary> word is just the <kanji>black</kanji> kanji you already know, standing on its own with the meaning unchanged.
items.reading_mnemonic: Over the village built on the fire pit, a <reading>crow</reading> lands on a smoking roof and caws <reading>くろ</reading>, so sooty now that it matches every roof and paddy: all <vocabulary form="黒">black</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この色は黒です。
example_sentences.english: This color is black.
example_sentences.furigana: この色[いろ]は黒[くろ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 黒い犬がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a black dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 黒[くろ]い犬[いぬ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 黒い靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought black shoes.
example_sentences.furigana: 黒[くろ]い靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 熱（あつ）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Here the <kanji>heat</kanji> is trapped inside one solid thing, like a mug, a pan handle, or a feverish forehead. The closing い makes it an adjective for that object being <vocabulary>hot (object)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grab the iron kettle on Grandma Kane's stove and your hand jerks back with a sharp <reading>ah-tsoo-ee</reading>. That burnt-finger yelp is 「<reading>あつい</reading>」, the word for a thing that is <vocabulary>hot (object)</vocabulary> to the touch.

example_sentences.japanese: このお茶は熱いです。
example_sentences.english: This tea is hot.
example_sentences.furigana: このお茶[ちゃ]は熱[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 熱いコーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink hot coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 熱[あつ]いコーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 熱いご飯を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat hot rice.
example_sentences.furigana: 熱[あつ]いご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A museum audio guide has one narrator with one flat tone, sighing <reading>'Sue, ma, run, aye'</reading> at every single painting. Forty rooms of that drone is <vocabulary>boring</vocabulary> boiled down, and <reading>つまらない</reading> is the sound the sigh already makes.

example_sentences.japanese: この本はつまらない。
example_sentences.english: This book is boring.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]はつまらない。

example_sentences.japanese: つまらない映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a boring movie.
example_sentences.furigana: つまらない映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日学校はつまらない。
example_sentences.english: School is boring every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]学[がっ]校[こう]はつまらない。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 楽（たの）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>music</kanji> those ice beads shake out of the bare branches turns a cold walk into something <vocabulary>fun / enjoyable</vocabulary>. That final い is what makes it an adjective.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the cold walk, <reading>Tano, she</reading> shakes every bare branch so the ice beads ring out their music, and she sings <reading>たのしい</reading> because the walk is suddenly <vocabulary form="楽しい">fun</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の学校は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: School is fun today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の学[がっ]校[こう]は楽[たの]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と映画を見るのは楽しい。
example_sentences.english: Watching a movie with friends is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]るのは楽[たの]しい。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は公園で遊ぶと楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: Playing in the park on the weekend is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]ぶと楽[たの]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 近（ちか）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>near</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>near</vocabulary> word are the same character. Adding the い on the end just turns it into an adjective.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a <reading>cheeky</reading> kid points at the vending machine just one switchback up and crows <reading>ちかい</reading>, because the drink you thought was an hour away is <vocabulary form="近い">near</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: うちはスーパーに近い。
example_sentences.english: My place is near the supermarket.
example_sentences.furigana: うちはスーパーに近[ちか]い。

example_sentences.japanese: あの銀行は駅に近い。
example_sentences.english: That bank over there is near the station.
example_sentences.furigana: あの銀[ぎん]行[こう]は駅[えき]に近[ちか]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は近い店で昼ご飯を食べる。
example_sentences.english: Today I'll eat lunch at a nearby shop.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You order a hot coffee at Koichi's konbini and it arrives the following Tuesday, cold, with a note apologising. Nobody waits a week for coffee unless the service is <vocabulary>slow / late</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 私（わたし）.
items.mnemonic_text: 'What, ah, she?' — no, watashi means I.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>private</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>I / me</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Behind the grain stalk, a shy farmer named <reading>Wattashee</reading> hugs the one seed sealed in its cocoon and whispers <reading>わたし</reading>: it belongs to <vocabulary form="私">me</vocabulary> alone.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は明日、友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I will watch a movie with my friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: My room is cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はコーヒーを飲みません。
example_sentences.english: I don't drink coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はコーヒーを飲[の]みません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 私（わたし）＋たち.
items.mnemonic_text: watashi plus tachi: I and my group, we.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each <kanji>private</kanji> stash belongs to one person, but stand a whole row of them side by side and that row becomes <vocabulary>we</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 私 reads わたし, so adding たち turns <vocabulary>we</vocabulary> into <reading>わたしたち</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: We watch movies.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは明日学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: We're going to school tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは明日[あした]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは一緒に遊びます。
example_sentences.english: We play together.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは一[いっ]緒[しょ]に遊[あそ]びます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 弟（おとうと）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the smallest hiker races ahead of everyone and falls straight into the vending machine at the top. That reckless little kid is exactly a <vocabulary>younger brother</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the smallest hiker races ahead making <reading>auto</reading> engine noises and yelling 「<reading>おとうと</reading>」 until he crashes into the vending machine, a true <vocabulary form="弟">younger brother</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の弟は学生です。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother is a student.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の弟[おとうと]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟と公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the park with my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は毎晩本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother reads a book every night.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 兄（きょう）＋弟（だい）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>older brother</kanji> and a <kanji>younger brother</kanji> together are what everyone calls <vocabulary>siblings</vocabulary>.
items.description: Covers siblings in general, including sisters, even though both kanji individually mean brother.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の兄弟は学生です。
example_sentences.english: My siblings are students.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の兄[きょう]弟[だい]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄弟と一緒に映画を見る。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie with my siblings.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[きょう]弟[だい]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に兄弟と遊ぶ。
example_sentences.english: I hang out with my siblings on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に兄[きょう]弟[だい]と遊[あそ]ぶ。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 医（い）＋者（しゃ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Whoever pulls the arrow out and shuts it away already practices <kanji>medicine</kanji>. Add the <kanji>person</kanji> doing it and you have a <vocabulary>doctor</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、医者に行きます。

example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、医[い]者[しゃ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 医者は今、忙しいです。

example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]は今[いま]、忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に医者を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I'll wait for the doctor with my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に医[い]者[しゃ]を待[ま]ちます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 彼（かれ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>he</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> are exactly the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker points at a shape trudging up and asks <reading>かれ</reading>. It sounds just like <reading>car, eh</reading>, and she means only the <vocabulary>he / boyfriend</vocabulary> who promised to meet her there.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は学生です。
example_sentences.english: He's a student.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼と一緒に映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie with him.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は今日家に帰ります。
example_sentences.english: He's going home today.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 彼（かの）kun'yomi ＋ 女（じょ）on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>he</kanji> walking off down the road turns out to be a <kanji>woman</kanji>, and now she's the one you point at and simply call <vocabulary>she / girlfriend</vocabulary>.
items.description: Context decides the sense: introduced as someone's partner it means girlfriend, used as a plain pronoun it just means she.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: She reads books.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は彼女と公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the park with her.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は彼[かの]女[じょ]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は今忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: She's busy right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は今[いま]忙[いそが]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 姉（あね）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports day, one loud kid bosses even the coaches around and nobody dares stop her. That commanding energy is exactly an <vocabulary>(my) older sister</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's sports day, a coach asks to change the relay order, and your bossy <vocabulary form="姉">older sister</vocabulary> answers 「<reading>あね</reading>」, a flat '<reading>ah, nah</reading>', and nobody dares argue.

example_sentences.japanese: 姉は今忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: My older sister is busy right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]は今[いま]忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 姉と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie with my older sister.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 姉は学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: My older sister goes to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 姉[あね]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — おねえさん cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of お姉さん.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A lost traveler at the riverbank asks a young woman for directions, calling her <vocabulary>older sister (polite)</vocabulary> before he even learns her name.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the lost traveler stretches his polite 「<reading>おねえさん</reading>」 into a long horse-like <reading>neigh</reading>, asking the way from a young woman he has never met but calls <vocabulary form="お姉さん">older sister</vocabulary>.
items.description: Use お姉さん for any young woman addressed politely — a shop clerk, a stranger — not only an actual older sister.

example_sentences.japanese: あなたのお姉さんは先生です。
example_sentences.english: Your older sister is a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: あなたのお姉[あね]さんは先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: お姉さんと一緒にご飯を食べます。

example_sentences.furigana: お姉[あね]さんと一[いっ]緒[しょ]にご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: お姉さんは明日学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: Older sister is going to school tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: お姉[あね]さんは明日[あした]学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — おじ cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 叔父.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A backup <kanji>father</kanji> who shows up every holiday, spoils you rotten, and sneaks you extra sweets is your <vocabulary>uncle</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every holiday the backup dad sneaks you so many extra sweets that your parents gasp '<reading>oh, gee</reading>', the <reading>おじ</reading> sound that follows your spoiling <vocabulary form="叔父">uncle</vocabulary> everywhere.
items.description: An uncle younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父と公園で遊んだ。
example_sentences.english: I played with my uncle at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]と公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだ。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、叔父の家に行く。

example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]、叔父[おじ]の家[いえ]に行[い]く。

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父は毎日お茶を飲む。

example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]は毎[まい]日[にち]お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — おば cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 叔母.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mother</kanji> figure who's still just a <kanji>youth</kanji> herself, holding kids anyway, is your <vocabulary>aunt</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still a youth herself, your <vocabulary form="叔母">aunt</vocabulary> holds the little cousins on her lap anyway and calms them with one squeaky <reading>oboe</reading> note that sounds just like <reading>おば</reading>.
items.description: An aunt younger than your parent; an older one uses different kanji, same reading.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の叔母[おば]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

items.reading_composition: Irregular — きのう cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 昨日.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>day</kanji> that already slipped past you, gone before you could grab it, is <vocabulary>yesterday</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You lunge for the day slipping past, but it locks its door with a rusty <reading>key</reading> that clicks <reading>きのう</reading>, and it is already <vocabulary form="昨日">yesterday</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a movie yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日友達と遊びました。

example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びました。

items.reading_mnemonic: Counting back one more day past yesterday, you find the <reading>otter toy</reading> you lost, still tagged <reading>おととい</reading>: <vocabulary form="一昨日">the day before yesterday</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 一昨日友達と遊びました。
example_sentences.english: I hung out with a friend the day before yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いっ]昨[さく]日[ひ]友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一昨日は忙しかったです。
example_sentences.english: I was busy the day before yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いっ]昨[さく]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しかったです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 昼（ひる）.

example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は公[こう]園[えん]で昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昼ご飯を一緒に食べませんか。
example_sentences.english: Would you like to eat lunch together?
example_sentences.furigana: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を一[いっ]緒[しょ]に食[た]べませんか。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 祖（そ）＋父（ふ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ancestor</kanji> still recent enough to be someone's <kanji>father</kanji> is exactly your <vocabulary>(my) grandfather</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.english: I play with my grandfather at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は祖[そ]父[ふ]と公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、祖[そ]父[ふ]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>mother</kanji> already holds two children tight in her lap. Give her enough years to also be an <kanji>ancestor</kanji>, and she's your <vocabulary>(my) grandmother</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の祖母は本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My grandmother reads books.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の祖[そ]母[ぼ]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に祖[そ]母[ぼ]と公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.english: Yesterday I met my grandmother.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、祖[そ]母[ぼ]に会[あ]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 首（くび）.

example_sentences.japanese: 首が寒いです。

example_sentences.furigana: 首[くび]が寒[さむ]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>ill</kanji> body checks into the one <kanji>institution</kanji> built to house the sick until they mend, and that building is a <vocabulary>hospital</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は病院で本を読みます。

example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は病[びょう]院[いん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 紙（かみ）.

items.reading_mnemonic: Cammy the goat eats anything, but what she loves most is <vocabulary>paper</vocabulary>. Hand her a page and <reading>Cammy</reading> grinds it to pulp, bleating <reading>かみ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は紙を買います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You fill a sheet of <kanji>paper</kanji> with words in your own <kanji>hand</kanji>, then fold it up and mail it. What lands in the far mailbox is a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日彼女に手紙を書いた。
example_sentences.english: I wrote her a letter yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]彼[かの]女[じょ]に手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]いた。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日父の手紙を読む。
example_sentences.english: I read Dad's letters every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]父[ちち]の手[て]紙[がみ]を読[よ]む。

example_sentences.japanese: この手紙は難しい。
example_sentences.english: This letter is difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: この手[て]紙[がみ]は難[むずか]しい。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 窓（まど）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Punch a square hole in a solid wall and fill it with a sheet of glass. Now you can watch the storm without a single drop landing on you, and that glass-filled square you stare through is a <vocabulary>window</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>mad doe</reading> out in the storm stares at you through the glass-filled square in the wall, rain streaming down her face but never yours, and you name that <vocabulary form="窓">window</vocabulary> 「<reading>まど</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: どの窓を開けますか。
example_sentences.english: Which window will you open?
example_sentences.furigana: どの窓[まど]を開[あ]けますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は窓から海を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the sea from the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は窓[まど]から海[うみ]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 寒いので、窓を閉めます。
example_sentences.english: It's cold, so I'm closing the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 寒[さむ]いので、窓[まど]を閉[し]めます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 歯（は）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini keeps a shelf of rock-hard rice crackers right by the till. Every year a customer bites down wrong and leaves a chipped <vocabulary>tooth</vocabulary> on the counter.
items.reading_mnemonic: The konbini night clerk answers every joke with one flat <reading>ha</reading>. That bark is your <reading>は</reading>, and it always flashes the gold <vocabulary>tooth</vocabulary> at the side of his grin.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の歯はいいです。
example_sentences.english: My teeth are fine.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の歯[は]はいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 歯でパンを食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat bread with my teeth.
example_sentences.furigana: 歯[は]でパンを食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 医者は私の歯を見ます。
example_sentences.english: The doctor looks at my teeth.
example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]は私[わたし]の歯[は]を見[み]ます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 痛（いた）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Step on a plug lying prongs-up in a dark room and the white spark that shoots up your foot is exactly <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary>. That final い marks it as an adjective.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi crosses the dark room, steps square on a plug lying prongs-up, and howls <reading>eye-tie</reading>, <reading>いたい</reading>, because that white spark shooting up his foot is <vocabulary form="痛い">painful</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 足が痛いです。
example_sentences.english: My foot hurts.
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]が痛[いた]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 歯が痛い。
example_sentences.english: My tooth hurts.
example_sentences.furigana: 歯[は]が痛[いた]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日からお腹が痛いです。
example_sentences.english: My stomach has been hurting since yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]からお腹[なか]が痛[いた]いです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 靴（くつ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The two leather cages you lock your feet into every morning, so you can stomp across gravel without a second thought, are your <vocabulary>shoes</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A barefoot hiker crosses the riverbank stones and picks up sharp <reading>cuts</reading> on both soles. She pulls on 「<reading>くつ</reading>」 so the next crossing scratches the <vocabulary>shoes</vocabulary>, not her feet.

example_sentences.japanese: この靴は高いです。
example_sentences.english: These shoes are expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この靴[くつ]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: デパートで靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought shoes at the department store.
example_sentences.furigana: デパートで靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 靴はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where are the shoes?
example_sentences.furigana: 靴[くつ]はどこですか。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 駅（えき）＋員（いん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone has to run the <kanji>station</kanji> where tired horses get swapped for fresh ones. That <kanji>employee</kanji>, one more mouth the station feeds, is the <vocabulary>station staff</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員に聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I'll ask the station staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は駅員です。
example_sentences.english: She's station staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は駅[えき]員[いん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日駅員に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met the station staff today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]駅[えき]員[いん]に会[あ]いました。

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 駅（えき）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>station</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>station</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で友達を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I wait for my friend at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 午後に駅へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the station in the afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]後[ご]に駅[えき]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で弁当を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a boxed lunch at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で弁[べん]当[とう]を買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 箱（はこ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Anything with six stiff flat sides and a lid you must lift before you can see what is inside is a <vocabulary>box</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hawk stalks round all six stiff sides of a shut <vocabulary form="箱">box</vocabulary>, screeching <reading>hah-koh</reading>, 「<reading>はこ</reading>」, until someone lifts the lid to show it what is inside.

example_sentences.japanese: この箱を開けてください。
example_sentences.english: Please open this box.
example_sentences.furigana: この箱[はこ]を開[あ]けてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は店で箱を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a box at the shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は店[みせ]で箱[はこ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 箱に本があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a book in the box.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]に本[ほん]があります。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 親（しん）＋切（せつ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>parent</kanji> who <kanji>cuts</kanji> the carrots on your plate into small, easy pieces is being <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary>. Treat it as a な adjective and slip な in before the noun it describes.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は親切な人です。
example_sentences.english: She is a kind person.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は親[しん]切[せつ]な人[ひと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は学生に親切です。
example_sentences.english: The teacher is kind to students.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は学[がく]生[せい]に親[しん]切[せつ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は私に親切でした。
example_sentences.english: My friend was kind to me.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は私[わたし]に親[しん]切[せつ]でした。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 聞（き）＋く.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hear</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to listen</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning carries over. Leaning your ear in to catch more is also how you ask someone a question.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon presses its ear to the crack in the gate, mutters <reading>key, coo</reading> once, then goes silent <vocabulary form="聞く">to listen</vocabulary>, breathing 「<reading>きく</reading>」 as voices drift through.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝ラジオを聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I listen to the radio every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]ラジオを聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に道を聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I ask a friend for directions.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に道[みち]を聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 母の声を聞きました。
example_sentences.english: I heard my mother's voice.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]の声[こえ]を聞[き]きました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 言（い）＋う.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>say</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean exactly the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: A fussy heron opens its small mouth and floats just one line of words up into the air, a sniffy 「<reading>いう</reading>」, <reading>ew</reading>, the only thing it ever bothers <vocabulary form="言う">to say</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はこれが好きだと言います。
example_sentences.english: She says she likes this.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はこれが好[す]きだと言[い]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は何と言いましたか。
example_sentences.english: What did the teacher say?
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は何[なに]と言[い]いましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はお茶を飲むと言いました。
example_sentences.english: My mother said she would drink tea.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]むと言[い]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 売（う）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Lay goods on the stand: uru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sell</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary> word are exactly the same, so they mean the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Face hidden under his cover, the proud samurai walks the road with a stuffed kangaroo, calling <reading>ooh, Roo</reading>, 「<reading>うる</reading>」, at every gate, since all that is left is <vocabulary form="売る">to sell</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は古い服を売ります。
example_sentences.english: My mother sells old clothes.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は古[ふる]い服[ふく]を売[う]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は駅で新聞を売ります。
example_sentences.english: He sells newspapers at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]で新[しん]聞[ぶん]を売[う]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: この店はパンを売りません。
example_sentences.english: This shop does not sell bread.
example_sentences.furigana: この店[みせ]はパンを売[う]りません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 走（はし）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your legs pump so fast the fence posts smear into one green line and your breath tears in and out. That is what it means to <vocabulary>run</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The coach has one <reading>harsh rule</reading>: keep going until the fence posts smear into one green line, so every kid has <vocabulary form="走る">to run</vocabulary>, gasping 「<reading>はしる</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝公園を走ります。
example_sentences.english: I run in the park every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]公[こう]園[えん]を走[はし]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は学校まで走りました。
example_sentences.english: He ran to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は学[がっ]校[こう]まで走[はし]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と駅まで走ります。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow, I will run to the station with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と駅[えき]まで走[はし]ります。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泳（およ）＋ぐ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A dog dropped into the river flattens out, paddles hard with all four legs, and pushes itself forward across the water. It has started to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A farmer tips a vat of yogurt down his front at the riverbank and wades in to rinse off. The current grabs him, and now he has to <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary>, spitting out <reading>oh, yogurt</reading>, which comes out as <reading>およぐ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝川で泳ぎます。
example_sentences.english: I swim in the river every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]川[かわ]で泳[およ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、友達と海で泳ぎます。
example_sentences.english: Today I swim in the sea with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、友[とも]達[だち]と海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬は海で泳ぎません。
example_sentences.english: I don't swim in the sea in winter.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]は海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぎません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 教（おし）＋える.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take something you know cold and load it, piece by piece, into a head that did not have it an hour ago. Doing that on purpose, until it sticks in the other person, is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A new student in the echoing hallway watches the tutor break every hard idea into clean steps and thinks, <reading>oh, she rules</reading>. The tutor smiles and says 「<reading>おしえる</reading>」, and handing knowledge over like that is what it means to <vocabulary>teach</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は学生に教える。
example_sentences.english: The teacher teaches the students.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は学[がく]生[せい]に教[おし]える。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は私に料理を教えます。
example_sentences.english: My mother teaches me how to cook.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は私[わたし]に料[りょう]理[り]を教[おし]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄は弟に泳ぐのを教えた。
example_sentences.english: My older brother taught my younger brother how to swim.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]は弟[おとうと]に泳[およ]ぐのを教[おし]えた。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 知（し）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once a fact is stuck to you firmly enough that you can produce it the second someone asks, it is yours. Carrying it around like that, always within reach, is what it means to <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>shrew</reading> keeps every fact stuck to its fur, always within reach, and squeaks 「<reading>しる</reading>」 as it hands one over the second you ask, which is what it means <vocabulary form="知る">to know</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は彼を知っています。
example_sentences.english: I know him.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は彼[かれ]を知[し]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: この道を知っていますか。
example_sentences.english: Do you know this road?
example_sentences.furigana: この道[みち]を知[し]っていますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は何も知りません。
example_sentences.english: She doesn't know anything.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は何[なに]も知[し]りません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 思（おも）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: A thought in the heart: omou.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You never reason this kind out; you just hold it, the way you cup a warm mug or trust a quiet hunch. Carrying an opinion around like that is to <vocabulary>think, to feel</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow cups a warm mug in her hooves, trusts a quiet hunch and lets out a soft <reading>oh, moo</reading>, 「<reading>おもう</reading>」, which is how you <vocabulary form="思う">feel</vocabulary> a thing without reasoning it out.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日行くと思う。
example_sentences.english: I think I'll go tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]行[い]くと思[おも]う。

example_sentences.japanese: この料理はおいしいと思う。
example_sentences.english: I think this dish is delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]はおいしいと思[おも]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は来ないと思う。
example_sentences.english: I don't think she'll come.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は来[こ]ないと思[おも]う。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a smooth green sapling out on the mountain trail for thirty years. Nobody prunes it, yet the trunk twists and <reading>gnarls</reading> on its own, and turning into something new like that is to <vocabulary>become</vocabulary> — <reading>なる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、先生になります。
example_sentences.english: Next year I'll become a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、先[せん]生[せい]になります。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が大きくなりました。
example_sentences.english: The cat got big.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が大[おお]きくなりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は会社員になった。
example_sentences.english: He became a company employee.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]になった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋つ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your two hands are the first pockets anyone ever had. Close your fingers around a thing and carry it off, and you <vocabulary>have</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Moe the furniture mover carries every crate up six flights himself, both arms wrapped tight around each one. Whatever you grip the way <reading>Moe totes</reading> a crate, you <vocabulary>hold</vocabulary> — <reading>もつ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本を持ちます。
example_sentences.english: I hold a book.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]を持[も]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はかばんを持っています。
example_sentences.english: She is holding a bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はかばんを持[も]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄はカメラを持たない。
example_sentences.english: My older brother doesn't have a camera.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]はカメラを持[も]たない。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 取（と）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Reach out, close your hand on something that was not yours a second ago, and pull it back to your chest. That motion, from start to finish, is what it means to <vocabulary>take</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You reached out, closed your hand on what was not yours a second ago and <reading>tore</reading> it back to your chest; that whole <reading>とる</reading> motion is to <vocabulary form="取る">take</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 机の本を取る。
example_sentences.english: I take the book on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の本[ほん]を取[と]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 塩を取ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please pass the salt.
example_sentences.furigana: 塩[しお]を取[と]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女が写真を取った。
example_sentences.english: She took a photo.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]が写[しゃ]真[しん]を取[と]った。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer will <reading>tuck a roo</reading> toy under one arm, clip its leash to a bag strap, and thumb its light-up eyes on in a single move. One motion that both fastens a thing and powers it up is <vocabulary>to turn on / attach</vocabulary> it, <reading>つける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 電気をつける。
example_sentences.english: I turn on the light.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]気[き]をつける。

example_sentences.japanese: テレビをつけました。
example_sentences.english: I turned on the TV.
example_sentences.furigana: テレビをつけました。

example_sentences.japanese: 手紙に切手をつける。
example_sentences.english: I attach a stamp to the letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]紙[がみ]に切[きっ]手[て]をつける。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（だ）＋す.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You grab the parcel wedged in the box and make it <kanji>exit</kanji> over the rim yourself. Forcing a thing up and out like that is to <vocabulary>take out / send</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You jab a feather <reading>duster</reading> under the parcel wedged in the box and lever it up over the rim with a <reading>だす</reading>, which is how you <vocabulary form="出す">take out</vocabulary> what is stuck.

example_sentences.japanese: かばんから本を出す。
example_sentences.english: I take a book out of my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんから本[ほん]を出[だ]す。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に手紙を出す。
example_sentences.english: I send a letter to a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に手[て]紙[がみ]を出[だ]す。

example_sentences.japanese: お金を出してください。
example_sentences.english: Please take out some money.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]を出[だ]してください。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 入（い）＋れる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take the coin and make it <kanji>enter</kanji> the narrow slot, pushing where it does not want to go. Doing the entering to something else, not yourself, is to <vocabulary>put in</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The coin slot on the <reading>eerie loo</reading> at the station jams, so you thumb the coin in hard, past where it wants to go, with a <reading>いれる</reading> clunk: that is to <vocabulary form="入れる">put in</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 箱に本を入れる。
example_sentences.english: I put the book in the box.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]に本[ほん]を入[い]れる。

example_sentences.japanese: お茶を入れます。
example_sentences.english: I'll make some tea.
example_sentences.furigana: お茶[ちゃ]を入[い]れます。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんに鍵を入れた。
example_sentences.english: I put the key in the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんに鍵[かぎ]を入[い]れた。

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 待（ま）＋つ.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary>wait</vocabulary> is to stand on the same rubber mat by the door so long that your shoes leave two pale dents in it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A station guard lines up spare floor <reading>mats</reading>, counts them, then lines them up again. It is the only thing to do while he <reading>まつ</reading> for the delayed train, so he has learned to <vocabulary>wait</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で友達を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I wait for my friend at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで待ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please wait here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで待[ま]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はバスを待っています。
example_sentences.english: She's waiting for the bus.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はバスを待[ま]っています。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 会（あ）＋う.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two friends round the same blind corner from opposite sides at a full run and <vocabulary>meet</vocabulary> forehead to forehead.
items.reading_mnemonic: The twins sprint round the corner and crack heads, and both yelp <reading>ow</reading>. That yelp is exactly how <reading>あう</reading> sounds on the day they finally <vocabulary>meet</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日友達に会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で彼女と会った。
example_sentences.english: I met her at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で彼[かの]女[じょ]と会[あ]った。

example_sentences.japanese: いつ先生に会いますか。
example_sentences.english: When will you meet the teacher?
example_sentences.furigana: いつ先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 入（はい）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>enter</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to enter</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. This is the intransitive one: you walk in under your own steam, nobody pushes you through the door.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leaning forward, one leg stepping ahead, you duck under the low doorway calling <reading>hi, Ruth</reading>, and on <reading>はいる</reading> you <vocabulary form="入る">enter</vocabulary> under your own steam.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は部屋に入ります。
example_sentences.english: I enter the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は部屋[へや]に入[はい]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は店に入った。
example_sentences.english: He entered the shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は店[みせ]に入[はい]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が家に入る。
example_sentences.english: The cat enters the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が家[いえ]に入[はい]る。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>exit</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to leave / go out</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. This is the intransitive one: you head out yourself, you are not shoved out by anyone.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>deer</reading> trapped in the lidless box stacks loose rocks into a little mountain and climbs out over the top, <reading>でる</reading>, to <vocabulary form="出る">leave</vocabulary> on its own hooves.

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、家を出ます。
example_sentences.english: I leave the house in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、家[いえ]を出[で]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は駅を出た。
example_sentences.english: He left the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]を出[で]た。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が部屋から出た。
example_sentences.english: The cat came out of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が部屋[へや]から出[で]た。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You jab in the number and cackle your hello far too loudly down the line. That <reading>cackle-rue</reading> of a greeting is <reading>かける</reading>, which is <vocabulary>to make a call</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は母に電話をかけます。
example_sentences.english: I call my mother.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は母[はは]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日友達に電話をかけた。
example_sentences.english: I called a friend yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]友[とも]達[だち]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけた。

example_sentences.japanese: 誰に電話をかけますか。
example_sentences.english: Who are you calling?
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]に電[でん]話[わ]をかけますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 止（と）＋まる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>stop</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary> are the same character, so the meaning carries over. The trailing kana marks the intransitive one: something halts on its own, with nobody stopping it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle plants one foot flat, heel and toes dug in, and his <reading>tomato</reading> basket sways, <reading>とまる</reading>, as he comes to a <vocabulary form="止まる">stop</vocabulary> on his own.

example_sentences.japanese: バスが止まる。
example_sentences.english: The bus stops.
example_sentences.furigana: バスが止[と]まる。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が止まった。
example_sentences.english: The rain stopped.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が止[と]まった。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで止まらないで。
example_sentences.english: Don't stop here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで止[と]まらないで。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 考（かんが）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: Turn it over in the mind: kangaeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take a hard problem, turn it over in your hands like a stuck jar lid, and work at it until it gives. That patient working-at-a-thing until it opens is to <vocabulary>think it through, to consider</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>kangaroo</reading> turns a stuck jar lid over and over in its paws, working at it until it gives with a 「<reading>かんがえる</reading>」, the patient way you <vocabulary form="考える">think</vocabulary> a problem through.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は明日のことを考える。
example_sentences.english: I think about tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は明日[あした]のことを考[かんが]える。

example_sentences.japanese: あなたはどう考えますか。
example_sentences.english: What do you think?
example_sentences.furigana: あなたはどう考[かんが]えますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 考える時間が欲しい。
example_sentences.english: I want some time to think.
example_sentences.furigana: 考[かんが]える時[じ]間[かん]が欲[ほ]しい。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 作（つく）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A crew at the riverbank ties loose reeds together until the heap becomes a raft that floats. Turning scattered junk into a thing that was not there an hour ago is <vocabulary>to make</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The riverbank boatwright never works alone. They <reading>took a crew</reading> of two, because <vocabulary>to make</vocabulary> <reading>つくる</reading> a whole canoe alone in one day is impossible.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は晩ご飯を作ります。
example_sentences.english: Mom makes dinner.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を作[つく]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日パンを作った。
example_sentences.english: I made bread yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]パンを作[つく]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に弁当を作る。
example_sentences.english: I make boxed lunches with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に弁[べん]当[とう]を作[つく]る。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 使（つか）＋う.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The lone vending machine on the mountain trail is there for one purpose. Feeding it a coin and pressing the button is what it means <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The trail farmer keeps <reading>two cows</reading> yoked behind the vending machine. When a snack jams, driving the pair in as a battering ram is all anyone has <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary> <reading>つかう</reading> up here.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこのペンを使います。
example_sentences.english: I use this pen.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はこのペンを使[つか]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はお金を使う。
example_sentences.english: She spends money.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はお金[かね]を使[つか]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日カメラを使った。
example_sentences.english: I used a camera yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]カメラを使[つか]った。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 始（はじ）＋まる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A race that the gun sends tearing off the line with nobody there to start it has simply come <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> all by itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the school sports field the gun cracks and the kangaroo the kids call Jim is already gone. Shout <reading>Ha, Jim, a roo</reading> and you have <reading>はじまる</reading>, a race that came <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> on its own.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校が八時に始まります。
example_sentences.english: School begins at eight.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]が八[はち]時[じ]に始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画が今始まります。
example_sentences.english: The movie is starting now.
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]が今[いま]始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が始まりました。
example_sentences.english: It started raining.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が始[はじ]まりました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 始（はじ）＋める.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You open the book, set the pace, and drive the class forward yourself, and making something start by your own hand like that is <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound in 始まる, so the one where you start something yourself is <reading>はじめる</reading>, <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本を読み始めます。
example_sentences.english: I begin reading a book.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]を読[よ]み始[はじ]めます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日から勉強を始めます。
example_sentences.english: I'll start studying from today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]から勉[べん]強[きょう]を始[はじ]めます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は映画を見始めた。
example_sentences.english: She started watching a movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]始[はじ]めた。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乗（の）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A badger in a peaked cap hauls itself up into the night bus and grabs the rail as the bus pulls away. That scramble up onto a moving vehicle is what it means to <vocabulary>board</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The badger's electric bus rolls up with <reading>no roar</reading> at all, so you almost miss it in the dark. Jump on before the doors close and you 「<reading>のる</reading>」 — you <vocabulary>ride</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はバスに乗ります。
example_sentences.english: I take the bus.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はバスに乗[の]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅でタクシーに乗りました。
example_sentences.english: I took a taxi at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]でタクシーに乗[の]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: どこでバスに乗りますか。
example_sentences.english: Where do you get on the bus?
example_sentences.furigana: どこでバスに乗[の]りますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 座（すわ）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sit</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to sit</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning carries straight across. The kana on the end only turns it into a verb.
items.reading_mnemonic: Rain <reading>swirls</reading> outside, so two shrine cats duck under the shelter, fold their legs side by side and purr 「<reading>すわる</reading>」 as they settle in <vocabulary form="座る">to sit</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: ここに座ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please sit here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに座[すわ]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は椅子に座ります。
example_sentences.english: He sits on the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は椅[い]子[す]に座[すわ]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫がベッドに座った。
example_sentences.english: The cat sat on the bed.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]がベッドに座[すわ]った。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 借（か）＋りる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You carry a neighbour's ladder home, use it for one afternoon, and promise it back by dark. Taking a thing on the promise you give it back is to <vocabulary>borrow</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You <reading>carry</reading> the neighbour's ladder home on one shoulder, calling <reading>かりる</reading> over the fence and promising it back by dark, which is what it is to <vocabulary form="借りる">borrow</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 本を借りる。
example_sentences.english: I'll borrow a book.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]を借[か]りる。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達から傘を借ります。
example_sentences.english: I'll borrow an umbrella from a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]から傘[かさ]を借[か]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で辞書を借りました。
example_sentences.english: I borrowed a dictionary at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で辞[じ]書[しょ]を借[か]りました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 降（お）＋りる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The chairlift on the mountain trail carries you up, and where the cable turns you <kanji>descend</kanji> from the seat onto the snow. That hop down off the lift is how you <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ori the lift attendant sighs <reading>'oh, really'</reading> at every skier who freezes on the unloading ramp. Only when they hear his flat 「<reading>おりる</reading>」 do they finally <vocabulary>get off</vocabulary> the chair.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は駅で降ります。
example_sentences.english: I get off at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は駅[えき]で降[お]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: バスを降りました。
example_sentences.english: I got off the bus.
example_sentences.furigana: バスを降[お]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: どこで降りますか。
example_sentences.english: Where do you get off?
example_sentences.furigana: どこで降[お]りますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 終（お）＋わる.
items.mnemonic_text: It comes to an end: owaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Follow a road all the way to its <kanji>end</kanji> and there is no more road left to walk. Something that runs itself out like that, with nobody stopping it, is <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You follow the road to where it runs out and find a walrus sprawled on the last stone; <reading>oh, walrus</reading>, you sigh, <reading>おわる</reading>, there is no more road and the walk can only <vocabulary form="終わる">finish</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校は三時に終わる。
example_sentences.english: School finishes at three.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]は三[さん]時[じ]に終[お]わる。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画が終わった。
example_sentences.english: The movie finished.
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]が終[お]わった。

example_sentences.japanese: 終わったら家に帰る。
example_sentences.english: When it finishes, I'll go home.
example_sentences.furigana: 終[お]わったら家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 貸（か）＋す.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A friend's phone is dead, so you unplug your charger and hand it over until lunch. Handing your own thing to someone else for a bit, knowing it comes back, is to <vocabulary>lend</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your friend offers you <reading>cash</reading> for the charger, but you just unplug it and hand it over till lunch with a <reading>かす</reading>, no money needed; you only <vocabulary form="貸す">lend</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は妹にペンを貸す。
example_sentences.english: I lend my younger sister a pen.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は妹[いもうと]にペンを貸[か]す。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生が辞書を貸した。
example_sentences.english: The teacher lent a dictionary.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]が辞[じ]書[しょ]を貸[か]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達にお金を貸しますか。
example_sentences.english: Will you lend money to a friend?
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]にお金[かね]を貸[か]しますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 渡（わた）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>ford</kanji> the shallow river stepping stone by stepping stone until you reach the far bank. Getting all the way to the other side is what it means to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each step the heron takes through the <reading>water</reading> makes a slow suck and slap, 「<reading>わたる</reading>」, as it works toward the other side. That patient wade is the bird choosing to <vocabulary>cross</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 道を渡ります。
example_sentences.english: I cross the street.
example_sentences.furigana: 道[みち]を渡[わた]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: あの橋を渡りました。
example_sentences.english: I crossed that bridge.
example_sentences.furigana: あの橋[はし]を渡[わた]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が川を渡る。
example_sentences.english: A child crosses the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が川[かわ]を渡[わた]る。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 切（き）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cut</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>to cut</vocabulary> word are the very same thing, so the る on the end just makes it the verb you do to something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit takes a sword to one carrot seven times, then <reading>keel</reading>s over giggling at the bits on the board, <reading>きる</reading>: that is what it means to <vocabulary form="切る">cut</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 母が野菜を切ります。
example_sentences.english: Mom cuts the vegetables.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が野[や]菜[さい]を切[き]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: この紙を切ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please cut this paper.
example_sentences.furigana: この紙[かみ]を切[き]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はパンを切った。
example_sentences.english: My little brother cut the bread.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はパンを切[き]った。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 洗（あら）＋う.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You hold a filthy boot under the tap and work every seam with your thumbs until the water finally runs clear. Driving grime off a thing with water is what it means to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's team tracks the whole muddy field into the hallway and kicks up <reading>a row</reading> over whose boots stink worst. Sei lines every boot at the tap, because someone has to <vocabulary>wash</vocabulary> the lot, and mutters 「<reading>あらう</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝手を洗います。
example_sentences.english: I wash my hands every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]手[て]を洗[あら]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は毎日髪を洗う。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister washes her hair every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は毎[まい]日[にち]髪[かみ]を洗[あら]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は服を洗いました。
example_sentences.english: My mother washed the clothes.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は服[ふく]を洗[あら]いました。

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 歌（うた）＋う.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>song</kanji> sits silent on the page until a voice lifts it into the air. Pushing it out of your mouth like that is what it means to <vocabulary>sing</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The song lies silent on the page until you lift it into the air, ending on a proud <reading>you-ta-daa</reading>, <reading>うたう</reading>, and that push of voice is to <vocabulary form="歌う">sing</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は上手に歌う。
example_sentences.english: She sings well.
