example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]から駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いて二[に]十[じゅう]分[ふん]掛[か]かります。

example_sentences.japanese: 引っ越すのに、お金がたくさん掛かりました。
example_sentences.english: Moving cost a lot of money.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]すのに、お金[かね]がたくさん掛[か]かりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋には母の絵が掛かっています。
example_sentences.english: My mother's painting hangs in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]には母[はは]の絵[え]が掛[か]かっています。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 掛（か）＋ける.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach up and set the frame on the nail yourself; you choose to put a full hour into the work. Doing either by your own hand is to <vocabulary form="掛ける">hang</vocabulary> a thing or spend the time on it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 掛かる, so its hands-on twin <vocabulary form="掛ける">to hang or spend</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 帰ったら、コートはここに掛けてください。
example_sentences.english: When you get home, hang your coat here.
example_sentences.furigana: 帰[かえ]ったら、コートはここに掛[か]けてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はいつも椅子に服を掛けておきます。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother always leaves his clothes hanging over the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はいつも椅[い]子[す]に服[ふく]を掛[か]けておきます。

example_sentences.japanese: この料理には時間を掛けました。
example_sentences.english: I put a lot of time into this dish.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]には時[じ]間[かん]を掛[か]けました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋なる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Loose sheets keep drifting down onto each other with no hand guiding them, and the stack grows <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> as each one lands. Left to themselves they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> and settle into a pile.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dancer clacks her <reading>castanets</reading> over the desk, and with every clack another loose sheet drifts down onto the last until they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> in a heavy pile: <reading>かさなる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議と約束の時間が重なってしまいました。
example_sentences.english: The meeting ended up at the same time as my appointment.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]と約[やく]束[そく]の時[じ]間[かん]が重[かさ]なってしまいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上に本が重なっています。
example_sentences.english: Books are piled up on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に本[ほん]が重[かさ]なっています。

example_sentences.japanese: 仕事が重なって、今週はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Work has piled up, so I'm very busy this week.
example_sentences.furigana: 仕[し]事[ごと]が重[かさ]なって、今[こん]週[しゅう]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 川（かわ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Those three flowing strokes are the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji, and the <vocabulary>river</vocabulary> word is that same character unchanged: one drawing, one meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A soggy dog hauls itself out where three streams flow side by side, then <reading>cower</reading>s on the bank whimpering <reading>かわ</reading> at the fast water the three make together, the <vocabulary form="川">river</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は川に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は川[かわ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が川で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: Children play in the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が川[かわ]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 川で魚を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I see fish in the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 川[かわ]で魚[さかな]を見[み]ます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 天（てん）＋気（き）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Heaven</kanji> picks an <kanji>energy</kanji> level every morning. Whether it comes out sparking and stormy or flat and grey, that level is the <vocabulary>weather</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の天気はいいです。
example_sentences.english: Today's weather is nice.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の天[てん]気[き]はいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日はどんな天気ですか。
example_sentences.english: What kind of weather will it be tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]はどんな天[てん]気[き]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 天気がいいから公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: The weather's nice, so I'm going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 天[てん]気[き]がいいから公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 犬（いぬ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The animal that hears your car three streets away and is losing its mind at the door before your key is out is a <vocabulary>dog</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Your car is heard three streets away, and by the time your key is out the thing behind the door yelps <reading>a new</reading> arrival, <reading>いぬ</reading>, again and again. That furry doorbell is your <vocabulary form="犬">dog</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の犬は公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: My dog plays in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の犬[いぬ]は公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は犬の写真を見ます。
example_sentences.english: She looks at a photo of a dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は犬[いぬ]の写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 兄の犬は肉を食べます。
example_sentences.english: My older brother's dog eats meat.
example_sentences.furigana: 兄[あに]の犬[いぬ]は肉[にく]を食[た]べます。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 写（しゃ）＋真（しん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A copy of the truth: shashin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Freeze one moment as a <kanji>true</kanji> copy, exact enough that nobody can deny it happened. That undeniable copy of real life is a <vocabulary>photograph</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: これは私の家族の写真です。
example_sentences.english: This is a photo of my family.
example_sentences.furigana: これは私[わたし]の家[か]族[ぞく]の写[しゃ]真[しん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、友達の写真を見ました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday I looked at my friend's photos.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、友[とも]達[だち]の写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の写真はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is her photo?
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の写[しゃ]真[しん]はどこですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 冬（ふゆ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your breath shows indoors and the puddles wear a lid of ice by morning. The days shrink to a short grey window, and that hard still stretch is <vocabulary>winter</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leaving work, a commuter finds only a <reading>few</reading> minutes of grey light left in the sky and grumbles 「<reading>ふゆ</reading>」 at the dark. The season that keeps trimming every day down to nothing is <vocabulary>winter</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 冬の朝は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: Winter mornings are cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]の朝[あさ]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬に友達と山へ行く。
example_sentences.english: In winter I go to the mountains with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]に友[とも]達[だち]と山[やま]へ行[い]く。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬は家で映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: In winter I watch movies at home.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]は家[いえ]で映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 古（ふる）＋い.
items.mnemonic_text: Ten mouths of old stories: furui.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>old</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>old (thing)</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so they carry the very same meaning. The closing い is the adjective marker, and it sits on every い adjective without exception.
items.reading_mnemonic: The mouth that has counted to ten every morning for centuries has grown a <reading>furry</reading> grey beard of dust, and it mumbles <reading>ふるい</reading> between numbers, as <vocabulary form="古い">old</vocabulary> as the counting itself.

example_sentences.japanese: これは古い本です。
example_sentences.english: This is an old book.
example_sentences.furigana: これは古[ふる]い本[ほん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 古い靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought old shoes.
example_sentences.furigana: 古[ふる]い靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの橋は古いです。
example_sentences.english: That bridge over there is old.
example_sentences.furigana: あの橋[はし]は古[ふる]いです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 忙（いそが）＋しい.
items.mnemonic_text: No room in the heart: isogashii.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You are cooking on every burner when the phone starts ringing and both oven timers go off. Never finishing one job before the next lands on you is <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: With every burner going, the phone ringing and both oven timers shrieking, Sora gasps <reading>'Easy, gosh, gee'</reading> at anyone who asks. That gasp, <reading>いそがしい</reading>, means <vocabulary form="忙しい">busy</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I'm busy today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は会社で忙しい。
example_sentences.english: My dad is busy at the office.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は会[かい]社[しゃ]で忙[いそが]しい。

example_sentences.japanese: 忙しいから行きません。
example_sentences.english: I won't go because I'm busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 忙[いそが]しいから行[い]きません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 低（ひく）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The limbo bar at school keeps dropping until it sits so <vocabulary>low</vocabulary> that even the cat cannot slink under it. The final い just marks it as an adjective, the badge every い adjective wears.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school limbo contest the bar sinks so <vocabulary form="低い">low</vocabulary> that the cat gets stuck under it, and the kid bending back next lets out a nervous <reading>hiccup</reading>, <reading>ひくい</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: この椅子は低いです。
example_sentences.english: This chair is low.
example_sentences.furigana: この椅[い]子[す]は低[ひく]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 低いテーブルを買います。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to buy a low table.
example_sentences.furigana: 低[ひく]いテーブルを買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は低いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain over there is low.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は低[ひく]いです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 良（よ）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the plain word for good pulling on a stiff, pressed suit. The い ending still makes it an adjective, but that starch is what turns it into <vocabulary>good (formal)</vocabulary>, the version for letters and speeches.
items.reading_mnemonic: Buttoned into its stiff pressed suit, the plain everyday word climbs to the podium for a speech and opens with a dignified <reading>yo-eee</reading>, <reading>よい</reading>, the starched way of saying <vocabulary form="良い">good</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は良いです。
example_sentences.english: This room is nice.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は良[よ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は良い人です。
example_sentences.english: She is a good person.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は良[よ]い人[ひと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: お茶を飲んでも良いですか。
example_sentences.english: May I have some tea?
example_sentences.furigana: お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでも良[よ]いですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 雨（あめ）.
items.mnemonic_text: Drops from the sky frame: ame.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You have met this shape already: the <kanji>rain</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>rain</vocabulary> word are the very same character, so the meaning does not shift at all.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Amy</reading> presses her nose to the window under the flat roof and counts the four dashes falling down each side of the glass, calling every one 「<reading>あめ</reading>」, the <vocabulary form="雨">rain</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は雨です。
example_sentences.english: It's raining today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨で傘を買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll buy an umbrella because of the rain.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]で傘[かさ]を買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 夕方から雨が来ます。
example_sentences.english: It'll start raining in the evening.
example_sentences.furigana: 夕[ゆう]方[がた]から雨[あめ]が来[き]ます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 春（はる）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You give up on a bare brown branch as dead wood. A week later it is covered in green buds, and that overnight comeback is <vocabulary>spring</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Gardener <reading>Harold</reading> nearly saws off the bare brown branch as dead wood, then spots green buds on it a week later and gasps <reading>はる</reading>: the branch is back, and so is <vocabulary form="春">spring</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 春はいい天気です。
example_sentences.english: Spring has nice weather.
example_sentences.furigana: 春[はる]はいい天[てん]気[き]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は春に公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the park in spring.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は春[はる]に公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今年の春は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: This year's spring is enjoyable.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]の春[はる]は楽[たの]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 秋（あき）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The leaves let their green drain out, go the colour of dry straw, and drop. Crops come in, the evenings turn sharp, and that long wind-down is <vocabulary>autumn</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A caretaker at the school rakes a mat of fallen leaves off the running track, every one the same dull <reading>khaki</reading>, and grunts 「<reading>あき</reading>」. The season that strips the trees and browns the field is <vocabulary>autumn</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今年の秋は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: This year's autumn is cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]の秋[あき]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 秋に友達と公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play at the park with a friend in autumn.
example_sentences.furigana: 秋[あき]に友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 秋の果物はおいしいです。
example_sentences.english: Autumn fruit is delicious.
example_sentences.furigana: 秋[あき]の果物[くだもの]はおいしいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 夏（なつ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: By breakfast your shirt is stuck to your back and the ice in your glass is gone in a minute. When the sun is still glaring at eight at night, it is <vocabulary>summer</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At eight at night the sun is still glaring, and a cloud of <reading>gnats</reading> sticks to your sweaty shirt and drowns in your melted ice. You swat and mutter <reading>なつ</reading>, because that is <vocabulary form="夏">summer</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今年の夏は暑いです。
example_sentences.english: This summer is hot.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]の夏[なつ]は暑[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 夏に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the sea in summer.
example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは夏に公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: We play at the park in summer.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは夏[なつ]に公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 高（たか）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tall / expensive</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary>tall / expensive</vocabulary> word are the same character with the same meaning. The final い just makes it an adjective, the ending every い adjective keeps.
items.reading_mnemonic: Out on the flat prairie, Kai leans from the one window of the lone lid-capped tower, and the crowd far below cheers <reading>Ta, Kai!</reading>, <reading>たかい</reading>, craning up at how <vocabulary form="高い">tall</vocabulary> it is.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain is tall.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この時計は高いです。
example_sentences.english: This watch is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この時計[とけい]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 高い靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought expensive shoes.
example_sentences.furigana: 高[たか]い靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 雪（ゆき）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Rain that dawdled on the way down until it froze arrives as soft white clumps on your collar. That heaped, silent pile is <vocabulary>snow</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A soft white clump slides off your collar and down your back, and the cold melt makes you groan 「<reading>ゆき</reading>」, because <vocabulary form="雪">snow</vocabulary> down the neck is <reading>yucky</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は雪です。
example_sentences.english: It's snowing today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は雪[ゆき]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 窓から雪を見る。
example_sentences.english: I watch the snow from the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から雪[ゆき]を見[み]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供が雪で遊ぶ。
example_sentences.english: The kids are playing in the snow.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]が雪[ゆき]で遊[あそ]ぶ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 猫（ねこ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: It shoves a glass off the table, watches it drop, holds your eye the whole time, then strolls away. That animal is a <vocabulary>cat</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: After shoving your glass off the table and holding your eye as it smashes, the <vocabulary form="猫">cat</vocabulary> strolls up your arm and drapes itself over your <reading>neck, oh</reading> so smugly, purring <reading>ねこ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫が魚を食べます。
example_sentences.english: The cat eats fish.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]が魚[さかな]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の猫はベッドで寝ます。
example_sentences.english: Her cat sleeps on the bed.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の猫[ねこ]はベッドで寝[ね]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で猫と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play with a cat at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で猫[ねこ]と遊[あそ]びます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 鳥（とり）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that can sit on a branch, let go, and still not fall is a <vocabulary>bird</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A squirrel copies what it saw on the branch, lets go, and drops, its tail <reading>tore</reading> on the twigs. Above it, the one that let go and never fell chirps <reading>とり</reading>: a <vocabulary form="鳥">bird</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で鳥を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a bird in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で鳥[とり]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 木に鳥が来ました。
example_sentences.english: A bird came to the tree.
example_sentences.furigana: 木[き]に鳥[とり]が来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は鳥の声を聞きました。
example_sentences.english: My little sister heard a bird's voice.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は鳥[とり]の声[こえ]を聞[き]きました。

items.word_type: な adjective, noun, の adjective
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 黄（き）＋色（いろ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The single <kanji>color</kanji> that screams warning on wasps, road signs, and hazard tape is <vocabulary>yellow</vocabulary>. It behaves as a な adjective, so you slot な in before whatever noun it describes.

example_sentences.japanese: この花は黄色です。
example_sentences.english: This flower is yellow.
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は黄[き]色[いろ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 黄色いシャツを買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a yellow shirt.
example_sentences.furigana: 黄[き]色[いろ]いシャツを買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: どれが黄色ですか。
example_sentences.english: Which one is yellow?
example_sentences.furigana: どれが黄[き]色[いろ]ですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 涼（すず）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Imagine stepping off baking pavement into the shade of a big tree, where a breeze is moving and your sweat dries in seconds. That pleasant, sigh-worthy drop in heat is <vocabulary>cool / refreshing</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, <reading>Sue's sheet</reading> hangs dripping between two poles while she naps behind it in the breeze off the water. She swears it is the only <reading>すずしい</reading> patch of shade for miles, and that damp, breezy shade is <vocabulary>cool / refreshing</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は涼しいです。
example_sentences.english: This room is cool.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は涼[すず]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園は朝涼しいです。
example_sentences.english: The park is cool in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]は朝[あさ]涼[すず]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 風が涼しいですね。
example_sentences.english: The wind feels cool, doesn't it?
example_sentences.furigana: 風[かぜ]が涼[すず]しいですね。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 帽（ぼう）＋子（し）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take a piece of full-size <kanji>headgear</kanji> and shrink it down to <kanji>child</kanji> size. What perches on one head now, light and small, is a <vocabulary>hat</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この帽子は安いです。
example_sentences.english: This hat is cheap.
example_sentences.furigana: この帽[ぼう]子[し]は安[やす]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 店で帽子を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a hat at the shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 店[みせ]で帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 帽子はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the hat?
example_sentences.furigana: 帽[ぼう]子[し]はどこですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 雲（くも）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi leaves a bag of cotton balls open by the till, the ceiling fan catches them, and a grey clump ends up hovering over the onigiri shelf where nobody can reach it. That floating, unreachable fluff is a <vocabulary>cloud</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon perched on Koichi's onigiri shelf coos 「<reading>くも</reading>」, <reading>coo-moh</reading>, at the grey cotton fluff the ceiling fan keeps spinning just out of reach, its own little <vocabulary form="雲">cloud</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 窓から雲を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the clouds from the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から雲[くも]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は雲がありません。
example_sentences.english: There are no clouds today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は雲[くも]がありません。

example_sentences.japanese: 雲が一つ出ました。
example_sentences.english: One cloud appeared.
example_sentences.furigana: 雲[くも]が一[ひと]つ出[で]ました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 湖（みずうみ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A puddle you step over and a river is gone before you look twice. Water that just lies there in one huge still sheet you could row across for an hour is a <vocabulary>lake</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A boy on the lakeshore is sure the flat water is a quiet old woman named <reading>Miz Oomi</reading>, and every morning he greets it with 「<reading>みずうみ</reading>」. The huge calm sheet he waves at is a <vocabulary>lake</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは湖に行きました。
example_sentences.english: We went to the lake.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは湖[みずうみ]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの湖を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw that lake over there.
example_sentences.furigana: あの湖[みずうみ]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 夏に友達と湖で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: In summer I play at the lake with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]に友[とも]達[だち]と湖[みずうみ]で遊[あそ]びます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 暑（あつ）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing い makes this word an adjective. Aim it at a day, a room, or a long grey August, and it says the air itself has turned <vocabulary>hot (weather)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Through a long grey August the air in every room thickens like <reading>a stew</reading>, and everyone sweating in it sighs <reading>あつい</reading>: the day itself has gone <vocabulary form="暑い">hot</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は暑いです。
example_sentences.english: It's hot today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は暑いです。
example_sentences.english: This room is hot.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は暑[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は暑いですか。
example_sentences.english: Will it be hot tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は暑[あつ]いですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 寒（さむ）＋い.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The final い makes this an adjective, so you can pin it straight onto a noun. Picture a flat grey sky with your breath hanging in the air and the puddles frozen hard, and that whole outdoor chill is <vocabulary>cold (weather)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Courier <reading>Sam</reading> slips across the frozen puddles under that flat grey sky, his breath hanging in the air as he groans <reading>さむい</reading>, because the whole morning is bitterly <vocabulary form="寒い">cold</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's cold today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は寒い。
example_sentences.english: This room is cold.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は寒[さむ]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬は寒いですね。
example_sentences.english: Winter is cold, isn't it?
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]は寒[さむ]いですね。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 悲（かな）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A kid watches a balloon slip its string and float up past the rooftops. There is nothing to chase and nothing to do, and that empty feeling is <vocabulary>sad</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kid's balloon slips its string and drifts up past the <reading>cannery</reading> roof, and Nana, on her break, can only watch it go. That empty <reading>かなしい</reading> feeling is <vocabulary form="悲しい">sad</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は悲しいです。
example_sentences.english: I'm sad today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は悲[かな]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: この映画は悲しいです。
example_sentences.english: This movie is sad.
example_sentences.furigana: この映[えい]画[が]は悲[かな]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 悲しい手紙を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read a sad letter.
example_sentences.furigana: 悲[かな]しい手[て]紙[がみ]を読[よ]みました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 暖（あたた）＋かい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Think of the first real afternoon of spring, when the sun has finally taken the edge off the air and you carry your coat instead of wearing it. That easy, sink-into-it heat is <vocabulary>warm</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On that first spring afternoon, a teacher with his coat over one arm loosens <reading>a taut tie</reading> as well and sighs <reading>あたたかい</reading>, because the sun has made the air easy and <vocabulary form="暖かい">warm</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は暖かいです。
example_sentences.english: This room is warm.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は暖[あたた]かいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 春の天気は暖かいです。
example_sentences.english: Spring weather is warm.
example_sentences.furigana: 春[はる]の天[てん]気[き]は暖[あたた]かいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 暖かいお茶を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink warm tea.
example_sentences.furigana: 暖[あたた]かいお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 緑（みどり）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Think of a forgotten conservatory where one unstoppable vine has swallowed the glass, the benches, and the watering cans, leaving nothing any colour but <vocabulary>green</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the forgotten conservatory the vine has turned the benches and watering cans into one <reading>meadow</reading>, and the gardener who steps inside can only whisper <reading>みどり</reading> at all that <vocabulary form="緑">green</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: このシャツは緑です。
example_sentences.english: This shirt is green.
example_sentences.furigana: このシャツは緑[みどり]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 緑の野菜を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat green vegetables.
example_sentences.furigana: 緑[みどり]の野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は緑の帽子を買いました。
example_sentences.english: She bought a green hat.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は緑[みどり]の帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 嬉（うれ）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A dog hears the leash come off its hook and understands a walk is coming. The whole body wags at once, and that full-body wag is <vocabulary>happy / glad</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: When the leash comes off its hook, the dog wags so hard its whole body knocks the <reading>relish</reading> jar off the counter. Reiko laughs <reading>うれしい</reading>, since nothing in the house is that <vocabulary form="嬉しい">happy</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に会えて嬉しいです。
example_sentences.english: I'm glad I got to see my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]えて嬉[うれ]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい靴が買えて嬉しい。
example_sentences.english: I'm glad I could buy new shoes.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]が買[か]えて嬉[うれ]しい。

example_sentences.japanese: 母の手紙が来て嬉しいです。
example_sentences.english: I'm glad a letter from my mother arrived.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]の手[て]紙[がみ]が来[き]て嬉[うれ]しいです。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 鍵（かぎ）.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every locked door has just one small metal shape that will turn it, and that shape is a <vocabulary>key / lock</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The landlord turns <reading>cagey</reading> when you ask which small metal shape will turn your locked door, mutters 「<reading>かぎ</reading>」 and pockets the only <vocabulary form="鍵">key</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この鍵でドアを開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the door with this key.
example_sentences.furigana: この鍵[かぎ]でドアを開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 鍵はかばんにあります。
example_sentences.english: The key is in the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 鍵[かぎ]はかばんにあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 家の鍵を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a house key.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]の鍵[かぎ]を買[か]いました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 難（むずか）＋しい.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The screw on the konbini door has a star, a slot, and a square all cut into one head. No tool Koichi owns can turn it, and a screw nothing turns is <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A moose takes the cashier job at Koichi's konbini and cannot press the till buttons with hooves. Every shift the <reading>moose cashier</reading> sighs that the work is <reading>むずかしい</reading>, which just means <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は難しいです。
example_sentences.english: This book is difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 難しい映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I'm watching a difficult movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 難[むずか]しい映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 新聞を読むのは難しい。
example_sentences.english: Reading the newspaper is difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[しん]聞[ぶん]を読[よ]むのは難[むずか]しい。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋ねる.
items.mnemonic_text: Stacking heavy loads on purpose: kasaneru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set plate on plate by hand, squaring each one on the last, every <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> disc pushing the stack down harder. Doing it on purpose like that is to <vocabulary form="重ねる">pile up</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 重なる, so its by-hand partner <vocabulary form="重ねる">to pile things up</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かさねる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 食べた後で、皿を重ねて台所に運んでください。
example_sentences.english: After eating, please stack the plates and carry them to the kitchen.
example_sentences.furigana: 食[た]べた後[あと]で、皿[さら]を重[かさ]ねて台[だい]所[どころ]に運[はこ]んでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 寒い日は、シャツを二枚重ねて着ます。
example_sentences.english: On cold days, I wear two shirts, one over the other.
example_sentences.furigana: 寒[さむ]い日[ひ]は、シャツを二[に]枚[まい]重[かさ]ねて着[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 箱を三つ重ねたら、猫がその上に座った。
example_sentences.english: When I stacked three boxes, the cat sat on top of them.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]を三[みっ]つ重[かさ]ねたら、猫[ねこ]がその上[うえ]に座[すわ]った。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 知（し）＋らせる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>know</kanji> a fact the moment your arrow thuds into the target. Firing that same fact into someone else's target is <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> them.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 知 is 「し」 back in 知る, so <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> someone is just <reading>しらせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議の場所が変わったことを、みんなに知らせるのを忘れた。
example_sentences.english: I forgot to tell everyone that the meeting place had changed.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]の場[ば]所[しょ]が変[か]わったことを、みんなに知[し]らせるのを忘[わす]れた。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんが生まれたら、姉は電話で知らせると言っていた。
example_sentences.english: My older sister said she'd call to let us know when the baby is born.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんが生[う]まれたら、姉[あね]は電[でん]話[わ]で知[し]らせると言[い]っていた。

example_sentences.japanese: 授業に遅れるときは、先生に知らせるほうがいいですよ。
example_sentences.english: If you're going to be late for class, you should let your teacher know.
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]に遅[おく]れるときは、先[せん]生[せい]に知[し]らせるほうがいいですよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 届（とど）＋け＋出（で）＋る.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="届">deliver</kanji> a completed form to the city office and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your hands for good; that is to <vocabulary form="届け出る">report</vocabulary> or file something officially.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を無くしたので、交番に届け出ました。
example_sentences.english: I lost my wallet, so I reported it at the police box.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を無[な]くしたので、交[こう]番[ばん]に届[とど]け出[で]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 引っ越したら、新しい住所を市に届け出なければなりません。
example_sentences.english: When you move, you have to report your new address to the city.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]したら、新[あたら]しい住[じゅう]所[しょ]を市[し]に届[とど]け出[で]なければなりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 会社を休むときは、前の日に届け出てください。
example_sentences.english: If you're taking a day off work, please file notice the day before.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]を休[やす]むときは、前[まえ]の日[ひ]に届[とど]け出[で]てください。

items.word_type: ichidan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 感（かん）＋じる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">emotion</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="感じる">to feel</vocabulary> word are the same; the added kana just turns that emotion into something you actively do.

example_sentences.japanese: 冬の朝、窓を開けたときに感じる冷たい風が好きです。
example_sentences.english: I love the cold air you feel when you open the window on a winter morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]の朝[あさ]、窓[まど]を開[あ]けたときに感[かん]じる冷[つめ]たい風[かぜ]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい町に引っ越してから、少し寂しく感じる日が多い。
example_sentences.english: Since moving to a new town, I often have days when I feel a little lonely.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい町[まち]に引[ひ]っ越[こ]してから、少[すこ]し寂[さび]しく感[かん]じる日[ひ]が多[おお]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 試験の前は、一時間がとても短く感じる。
example_sentences.english: Right before an exam, an hour feels really short.
example_sentences.furigana: 試[し]験[けん]の前[まえ]は、一[いち]時[じ]間[かん]がとても短[みじか]く感[かん]じる。

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 提（てい）＋出（しゅつ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Presenting (提) and putting out (出): to submit.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The finished report stays in your hands until you <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> it to the front desk and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your fingers onto the tray. Letting a document exit you and stay with the office is how you <vocabulary form="提出する">submit</vocabulary> it.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口で書類を提出しました。
example_sentences.english: I handed in the documents at the bank counter.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]で書[しょ]類[るい]を提[てい]出[しゅつ]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: 名前を書いてから提出してください。
example_sentences.english: Please write your name before you hand it in.
example_sentences.furigana: 名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]いてから提[てい]出[しゅつ]してください。

example_sentences.japanese: テストを提出した後で、答えを一つ間違えたことが分かった。
example_sentences.english: After turning in the test, I realized I'd gotten one answer wrong.
example_sentences.furigana: テストを提[てい]出[しゅつ]した後[あと]で、答[こた]えを一[ひと]つ間[ま]違[ちが]えたことが分[わ]かった。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 申（もう）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A humble mouth speaking upward: mousu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You bend low and aim your words at the floor near an important person's feet, so they reach that person from below. Speaking from down there, kept small on purpose, is to <vocabulary form="申す">say something humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Bowed so low your words land by the chairman's feet, you speak up to him like a <reading>mouse</reading> squeaking from the floor: <reading>もうす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="申す">say</vocabulary> something humbly.

example_sentences.japanese: はじめまして、山田と申します。
example_sentences.english: Nice to meet you. My name is Yamada.
example_sentences.furigana: はじめまして、山田[やまだ]と申[もう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 母が「ありがとう」と申していました。
example_sentences.english: My mother asked me to tell you thank you.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]が「ありがとう」と申[もう]していました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一つ意見を申してもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: May I offer one opinion?
example_sentences.furigana: 一[ひと]つ意[い]見[けん]を申[もう]してもいいですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 参（まい）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Bowing low on the way: mairu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the car at the gate and walk the last stretch up to the house on foot, hat held in both hands. Coming toward someone that plainly, on foot and uncovered, is to <vocabulary form="参る">come to them humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: An old retainer waves away every offer of a ride, saying that walking to you in person is <reading>my rule</reading>, and sets off down the full length of the road. That slow arrival on your own two feet is <vocabulary form="参る">to go and come humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>まいる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の朝十時に、駅まで参ります。
example_sentences.english: I'll come to the station at ten tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の朝[あさ]十[じゅう]時[じ]に、駅[えき]まで参[まい]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 電車が参ります。危ないですから、下がってください。
example_sentences.english: A train is arriving. It's dangerous, so please step back.
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]が参[まい]ります。危[あぶ]ないですから、下[さ]がってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はすぐ参りますので、こちらの椅子に座ってください。
example_sentences.english: My mother will be right here, so please have a seat in this chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はすぐ参[まい]りますので、こちらの椅[い]子[す]に座[すわ]ってください。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 召（め）＋し＋上（あ）＋がる.
items.mnemonic_text: Calling something up to eat: meshiagaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored guest never fetches their own meal: the dishes are <kanji form="召">called for</kanji> from the kitchen and carried <kanji form="上">up</kanji> to the head of the table. Eating and drinking what has been summoned and raised to you is to <vocabulary form="召し上がる">eat or drink, honorifically</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: お茶とコーヒー、どちらを召し上がりますか。
example_sentences.english: Which would you like, tea or coffee?
example_sentences.furigana: お茶[ちゃ]とコーヒー、どちらを召[め]し上[あ]がりますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は昼ご飯に弁当を召し上がりました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher had a boxed lunch for lunch.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]に弁[べん]当[とう]を召[め]し上[あ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 熱いので、ゆっくり召し上がってください。
example_sentences.english: It's hot, so please take your time with it.
example_sentences.furigana: 熱[あつ]いので、ゆっくり召[め]し上[あ]がってください。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The white-gloved <reading>usher</reading> at the theatre glides over to walk each important guest in, out, and to their seat without a wasted step. That smooth, honored coming and going is <vocabulary form="いらっしゃる">to be, go, or come, honorifically</vocabulary>, and it sounds like <reading>いらっしゃる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来週、先生のご主人が日本にいらっしゃいます。
example_sentences.english: My teacher's husband is coming to Japan next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]、先[せん]生[せい]のご主[しゅ]人[じん]が日本[にほん]にいらっしゃいます。

example_sentences.japanese: おばあさんは今、庭にいらっしゃいますよ。
example_sentences.english: Grandma is out in the garden right now.
example_sentences.furigana: おばあさんは今[いま]、庭[にわ]にいらっしゃいますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: どちらからいらっしゃいましたか。

example_sentences.furigana: どちらからいらっしゃいましたか。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to speak: ossharu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever slow <reading>oh, sure</reading> the old retired professor mutters from his armchair, the whole class copies into their notes as settled fact. Giving a statement that weight because of who spoke it is <vocabulary form="おっしゃる">to say, honorifically</vocabulary>, and the sound is <reading>おっしゃる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: すみません、もっとゆっくりおっしゃってください。

example_sentences.furigana: すみません、もっとゆっくりおっしゃってください。

example_sentences.japanese: お名前は何とおっしゃいますか。

example_sentences.furigana: お名[な]前[まえ]は何[なに]とおっしゃいますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 奥さんは、この料理が一番おいしいとおっしゃいました。

example_sentences.furigana: 奥[おく]さんは、この料[りょう]理[り]が一[いち]番[ばん]おいしいとおっしゃいました。

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to do: nasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the grand duchess Nessa decides a thing will happen, it happens — <reading>Nessa rules</reading> the whole estate, and whatever task she takes on, she personally <vocabulary form="なさる">does the action, honorifically</vocabulary>. The sound of that lands as <reading>なさる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は何をなさいますか。
example_sentences.english: What are you doing this weekend?
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は何[なに]をなさいますか。

example_sentences.japanese: お父さんは日曜日も仕事をなさるんですか。

example_sentences.furigana: お父[とう]さんは日[にち]曜[よう]日[び]も仕[し]事[ごと]をなさるんですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、ご家族と旅行をなさるそうですね。

example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、ご家[か]族[ぞく]と旅[りょ]行[こう]をなさるそうですね。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 下（くだ）＋さる.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 医者が新しい薬を下さいました。

example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]が新[あたら]しい薬[くすり]を下[くだ]さいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父が古いカメラを下さいました。

example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]が古[ふる]いカメラを下[くだ]さいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨の中、迎えに来て下さって、本当に助かりました。

example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]の中[なか]、迎[むか]えに来[き]て下[くだ]さって、本[ほん]当[とう]に助[たす]かりました。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋せる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hanasu: able to speak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the nonstop <kanji form="話">talker</kanji> with the wagging tongue an open microphone and the words just pour out, no gap anywhere. Being able to let language run like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="話せる">be able to speak</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 話 is read 「はな」 from 話す, so <vocabulary form="話せる">can speak</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>はなせる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は英語が少し話せます。

example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は英[えい]語[ご]が少[すこ]し話[はな]せます。

example_sentences.furigana: 風邪[かぜ]で声[こえ]が出[で]ないので、今日[きょう]はあまり話[はな]せません。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬と話せたら、楽しいでしょうね。
example_sentences.english: It would be fun if I could talk with my dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]と話[はな]せたら、楽[たの]しいでしょうね。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kaku: able to write.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. The added ending only shifts it from doing the writing to being able to do it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is read 「か」 from 書く, so <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>かける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹はもうひらがなで自分の名前が書けます。

example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]はもうひらがなで自[じ]分[ぶん]の名[な]前[まえ]が書[か]けます。

example_sentences.english: This pen is old, but it still writes well.
example_sentences.furigana: このペンは古[ふる]いですが、まだよく書[か]けますよ。

example_sentences.japanese: チョークがないので、黒板に書けません。

example_sentences.furigana: チョークがないので、黒[こく]板[ばん]に書[か]けません。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 読（よ）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of yomu: able to read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="読">read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same meaning. The extra ending just moves it from reading to being able to read.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 読 is read 「よ」 from 読む, so <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>よめる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 使（つか）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of tsukau: usable.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new happens here: the <kanji form="使">use</kanji> kanji you already know is exactly what <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 「つか」 in 使う, so <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> just wears that same reading with a new tail: <reading>つかえる</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]が壊[こわ]れて使[つか]えないので、困[こま]っています。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of iku: able to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji stands on its own here, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> is that same kanji and not one idea more.

example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]なら、あの公[こう]園[えん]まで行[い]けるよ。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 来（こ）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kuru: able to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the burst rice grain scatters over the flat ground, the farmer asks his wife <reading>Cora, really?</reading> and she nods: a whole crop <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> up from that, <reading>こられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べられる.

items.reading_mnemonic: That 「た」 is the same one 食べる taught you earlier, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> is simply <reading>たべられる</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: 息子[むすこ]は辛[から]い料[りょう]理[り]が食[た]べられません。

example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は食[た]べられるんですか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 飲（の）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of nomu: able to drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: No story to build here: the <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> kanji is the whole word, and <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> means the very same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You know 「の」 already from 飲む, so <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> follows straight on as <reading>のめる</reading>.

example_sentences.furigana: このお茶[ちゃ]は熱[あつ]すぎて、まだ飲[の]めません。

example_sentences.furigana: この薬[くすり]はご飯[はん]の前[まえ]に飲[の]めますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋られる.

items.reading_mnemonic: This 「み」 is the reading you picked up in 見る, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>みられる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: このホテルの部屋から海が見られます。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋来（き）＋る.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Once every part has <kanji form="来">come</kanji> in, a finished thing <kanji form="出">exits</kanji> the far end of the line. That finished thing is proof the whole job was <vocabulary form="出来る">possible</vocabulary>.

example_sentences.japanese: この仕事は一人で出来ますか。
example_sentences.english: Can you handle this job on your own?
example_sentences.furigana: この仕[し]事[ごと]は一人[ひとり]で出[で]来[き]ますか。

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 走（はし）＋れる.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 会（あ）＋える.

items.reading_mnemonic: You already say 「あ」 this way in 会う, so <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> is nothing more than <reading>あえる</reading>.

items.reading_mnemonic: That 「か」 is the reading 買う already gave you, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> lands as <reading>かえる</reading>.
